title: The New Sounds
notes: - Fluttery bebop. Not unlike Giant Steps, but still mellow, listenable. Miles already sounds like himself--aloof and cool. Sonny Rollins sounds like a tickled deity. 4.20/5 stars. Would revisit.

title: Young Man With A Horn
notes: - Slower, a bit more melancholy, but still drives. Yesterdays hits like a dart to the gut. Solid overall, would've taken more JJ on the bone. 8.6/12. Will come back to it when I’m feeling wistful.

title: Blue Period
notes: - Light, breezy blues and bebop, apparently recorded during the New Sounds sessions. Not particularly noteworthy but perfectly fine. Would pair well with a G&T on a spring afternoon. 6/9.420 trumpets.

title: The Compositions of Al Cohn
notes: - Sorry Al but I don’t love these compositions. Musty pudding. 2/6 snack packs.

title: Miles Davis Volume 2
notes: - A mix of hard bop and slow jams. The ballads didn’t really do it for me but I liked the fast songs. The compositions are interesting and Art Blakey thumps like a madman on the skins. 7/11 Arnies.

title: Miles Davis Volume 3
notes: - Alright now we’re talking. Hard bop. A little funkier. Definitely my favorite so far.  Could listen to “It Never Entered My Mind” > “Well You Needn’t” on loop for hours. Horace Silver is a stanky warlock on the keys. B+/100. Would recommend.

title: Miles Davis Quartet
notes: - Sunny. Lyrical. With only 4 guys playing at a time, you get a lot more Miles. Love the way he sounds on this one. Pure, unadulterated. Elemental even. 4/5 planeteers. Praise be to mother Gaia.

title: Miles Davis All Star Sextet
notes: - Cool, bluesy tune followed by a quickier, boppier number. Arranged sections are almost cartoonish but the solos are solid. Miles is in full stride. JJ finally gets some room to breathe. Lucky Thompson sounds so velvety I blushed. Low eighties out of a hundred.

title: Miles Davis Quintet
notes: - Sounds like 2am in a Greenwich Village basement. Miles has his signature smokey tone. Don’t know this sax man but was pleasantly surprised. Sounds like Paul Desmond—clear and sparkly. Horace Silver and Kenny Clarke serve as the perfect compliments. High 16/20. Will keep in the rotation.

title: Miles Davis with Sonny Rollins
notes: - An all time great musical bromance. Love the way Miles sounds playing these intricate, Sonny-composed tunes. Rollins himself soars. Feels like I’m riding no hands over the Williamsburg bridge. 8.999…/10. Classic.

title: Miles Davis All Stars, Volume 1
notes: - Thelonious and Milt Jackson are in the mix and there’s an entirely new sound—cooler, blusier, more deliberate. I’ve always loved Bags’ Groove but not sure I ever appreciated what a leap forward it was. Swing Spring works perfectly on side B. A- overall. Fantastic stuff.

title: Miles Davis All Stars, Volume 2
notes: - Miles playing Thelonious compositions is one of my favorite things on earth and this recording of Bemsha Swing is probably my favorite instance of it. Love, love, love this song. The B side is a Gershwin tune, which is ok but feels a little out of place next to BS. Giving this album the same grade as the last one: A-.

title: The Musings of Miles
notes: - With the first 12”, we get about 15 extra minutes and a much more dynamic track list. Each song has a slightly different sound, yet it all hangs together. Miles often adopts a warm, tender tone. But not on Night in Tunisia, where he sounds somehow both haunted and at ease. Like a ghost who doesn’t mind being dead. A solid B overall.

title: Blue Moods
notes: - Gentle as a baby’s breath, cunning as the Serpent of Eden, these first two tracks sway, slither, and meander in a way that sounds unlike anything that’s come before. None of this works without Mingus, who shows us what happens when you put a genius on the bass. The B side is a bit more traditional, and for that reason a bit of a let down, but overall a great album. High B+.

title: Miles Davis and Milt Jackson Quintet/Sextet
notes: - Return to hard bop. Overall, more straightforward than the prior record, though the composed segments have a kind of alien eccentricity that really fists my bump. 4/5 Eridians.

title: Miles: The New Miles Davis Quintet
notes:
Just Squeeze Me starts playing.
Listener 1: "So as I was saying…"
Listener 2: "Wait. Shut up for a second. Was that John Coltrane?"
Listener 1: "Was it?"
Listener 2: "Not sure. That sax solo juiced like a plum, but it was so short. I almost missed it!"
Listener 1: "I'm sure we'll get another sax solo soon. Let's wait."
There Is No Greater Love starts and finishes. Listeners 1 and 2 exchange confused looks. How Am I To Know? starts. 94 long seconds pass. A saxophone blows.
Listeners 1 and 2, nodding in unison: "Niiice."

title: Collectors' Items
notes: A side was recorded in 1953 and has Bird alongside Rollins on sax. B side was recorded 3 years later, sans Bird. Maybe it speaks to some collectors, but this one’s not really my kinda tchotchke. 6/10 bored apes.

title: Cookin' With The Miles Davis Quintet
notes: The second release from the First Great Quintet, apparently recorded more-or-less live in the studio. I don’t really know what to say about this one except that these dudes rip. Miles sounds razor sharp. Trane is bending spacetime with every blow. Philly Joe and Red sound like conjoined twins who share a single brain. Easy A. We have 3 more from this crew and I can’t wait.

title: Miles Ahead
notes: Miles, the lone soloist, plays flugelhorn over subtle, impressionistic scores arranged by Gil Evans. It’s a radical departure from Cookin’s five-guys-jammin-in-the-studio aesthetic. Yet it’s undeniably beautiful. The backing ensemble includes 16 woodwind and brass instruments that at moments sound like strings. Miles converses like a shrewd interlocutor, knowing just when to interject, just how to ask, and just what to answer.

title: Birth of the Cool
notes: Recorded in 49 and 50 and released in 57,  it’s the seminal cool jazz album—hugely influential and historically very Important. It’s just not for me. I’ll give it a O for originality.

title: 'Round About Midnight
notes: The First Great Quintet is back! Well, technically, this was the first thing they ever recorded, but we’re listening to these in order of release date, so roll with it. This album has a lot of things I love—a Thelonious tune, plenty of Coltrane, Miles sounding smokier than Patty and Selma Bouvier—yet it doesn’t feel quite as inspired as Cookin’. Maybe the boys were still getting to know each other. Still a high grade: middle A-.

title: Agharta
notes: Surprise! 🥳 In honor of Miles’ 100th birthday, decided to throw on a bonus live album. It’s 1975’s Agharta. Though named for the mythic subterranean utopia, this one is nothing short of infernal. A fitting way to honor the great Prince of Darkness. Happy 100, Miles.

title: Relaxin' With The Miles Davis Quintet
notes: Another gerund from the FGQ. As the title suggests, these tunes are a bit more relaxed. Yet they still have plenty of vim. Some of the most lyrical playing thus far. This album gets bonus points because it has a Coltrane solo on every song. I get weak in the knee pits every time he starts. A.

title: Milestones
notes: The First Great Quintet plus Cannonball play a mix of styles, with an early example of modal work on the title track. With Adderley in the mix, Coltrane sounds better than ever. Like Duane and Dicky, Jayson and Jaylen, 3 Stacks and Big Boi, these two push each other to new heights. Apparently Red briefly stormed out of the studio after getting one too many notes from Miles, so Davis himself had to play piano on Sid’s Ahead. Chambers brings the bow out on Billy Boy. Trane melts face on Straight, No Chaser. Reasonable minds might disagree on where in the A range to place this one, but I’m gonna go dead center: 95/100. Great album name, btw. Best pun yet.

title: Jazz Track
notes: A side is a soundtrack. Not the most interesting thing to listen to on its own but it has its moments. B side is three recordings from the KOB sextet (complete with Mr. Bill Evans) before they recorded KOB. How these got relegated to the B side of a French soundtrack I do not know, but at any rate they are beautiful. 4/5 clopes. ***Post scriptum: Turns out this album was actually released two months *after* Kind Of Blue. That kinda helps explain why the sextet material was treated as an afterthought. Nevertheless, those tracks deserved better.

title: Porgy And Bess
notes: The second great Gil Evans callobo. Orchestral, proto-modal, you can hear intimations of Kind of Blue and everything that follows. Probably the best version of Summertime I’ve ever heard. If he had ended his career here he’d still be immortal. A+.

title: Kind Of Blue
notes: The undisputed heavyweight champion of the multiverse. The best of all possible albums. To hear it is to be enveloped by God’s infinite grace. Don’t forget to read (or re-read, if it’s been awhile) Bill Evans’ liner notes. Listen to it in mono.

title: Workin' With The Miles Davis Quintet
notes: Another gerund. We open with the definitive version of INEMM. I truly cannot overstate how much I love this rendition. It’s profound. It’s melonichalic. Each time Miles subtly subverts the melody, I groan in vicarious anguish. After that it’s mostly peppy, bluesy hard bop. Trane sounds as fiery as ever. Red, Paul, and Philly Joe get to showcase their chops on the hornless Ahmad’s Blues. And each side ends with a unique take of The Theme, a quick little diddy the band would use to close out their live shows. A overall.

title: Sketches Of Spain
notes: Gil y Miles otra vez. This one took me a few listens to get into. The Concierto, widely considered to be the centerpiece of the album, is impressive but meanders a bit too much for my taste. With Will O’ the Wisp we get a steadier rhythm and some fun, whimsical orchestration. The Pan Piper, with its circling motifs, sounds almost proto-minimalist, like Steve Reich before Steve Reich. Saeta is psychedelic before psychedelia. And then there’s Solea, an impassioned Phrygian masterpiece (and clearly an inspiration for Coltrane’s Ole, recorded a year later). It’s another A+.

title: Steamin' With The Miles Davis Quintet
notes: Four gerunds. Four rippers. Collectively they make up over two and a half hours of vital, life-affirming splendor. What. A. Series. This one, the fourth installment, features a delightful melange of styles—swinging mid-tempo, zippy bebop, wistful balladry—and it’s all dynamite. Really love the breakneck rendition of Well You Needn’t. Miles and Trane play maniacally out-of-sync on the head, and all four solos crank. Another easy A.

title: Someday My Prince Will Come
notes: A single bass note pulses. An ethereal piano glimmers. In glides Miles, playing Snow White, sounding as sinless as a newborn calf. They may call him the Prince of Darkness, but here, for a blissful few minutes, he has nothing to offer but warm, golden light. After that what we get is a very solid jazz album. Coltrane has only two appearances, but boy does he make them count. Elsewhere Hank Mobley fills his shoes as well as any mortal could. Wynton Kelly, on piano, sparkles. High A-.

title: Seven Steps To Heaven
notes: With a new cast of musicians, things sound a bit different. How exactly? Might need a few more listens to pin it down, but one thing I can say for certain is that Ron Carter is a god. His bass lines don’t just walk, they tap dance. Rather than keeping time, he adorns it. With him in the mix, everything sounds a little more fluid and free. It’s a low A- overall. Getting pumped for the Second Great Quintet.

title: Quiet Nights
notes: Another album with Gil. Has its moments but not my favorite. Bossa nova rhythms paired with orchestration doesn’t really work for me. A little too Tommy Bahama. B-.
